solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Abridged huge article in French, causing confusion

indicators.note: an abridged text has been cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: JUMBO means huge; shortened by one letter
LE is the French masculine definite article

explanation.surface: A shortened and garbled French text leaves its reader muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: JUMBO is the word for huge that gets cut short, and 'article in French' could be LE, LA or UN; LE fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A disordered mess or heap is a state of muddle, so the noun works as a synonym.

clue.text: Officer coming in shot cheating brother

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a jab is an injection, a shot

explanation.surface: A soldier is shot while arriving to deal with a treacherous sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' is a noun here, a jab or injection, not a past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis this twin tricked his elder sibling Esau out of his birthright and blessing.

clue.text: Theatre in Scottish island thus has closed early

indicators.note: something closed early stops before its end, so the word loses its last letter
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so what follows is enclosed by the word before

parts.note: Mull is an island of the Inner Hebrides
the word with its final letter removed

explanation.surface: A Scottish island theatre has shut up shop ahead of time.
explanation.walkthrough: The island is the outer piece and the rest goes inside it; 'thus' is the Latin word printers use to mark a quoted error as original.
explanation.definitionFit: A music hall is a venue for variety entertainment, a kind of popular theatre in Victorian Britain.

clue.text: Little room, note for diver

parts.note: the loo is the lavatory, the smallest room

explanation.surface: A cramped room with a note left for a scuba diver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little room' is a euphemism: in Britain the smallest room is the lavatory, the loo.
explanation.definitionFit: The loon is the North American name for the bird Britons call a diver, which hunts underwater.

clue.text: Officers, the first two each getting uniform

indicators.note: the first two letters of a word are its opening pair, so only those are kept

parts.note: apiece means each, as in a pound apiece

explanation.surface: Two senior officers are each issued with kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like a soldier's kit, continuing the officers picture, but it is the adjective meaning consistent.
explanation.definitionFit: Things of a piece are consistent or alike throughout, which is what uniform means as an adjective.

clue.text: Reasonable treatment, just a shortage of medicine?

indicators.note: a shortage means something is missing, so the word comes up one letter short

parts.note: a DOSE of medicine, missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A patient complains of fair care but too little medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: Fair dos (or fair do's) is British slang for fair treatment, a fair share.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom asks for equitable dealing, so it names reasonable, even-handed conduct toward someone.

clue.text: Purse containing zero — empty in sadly no time

indicators.note: sadly means badly or wretchedly, so the letters are knocked out of order
'no' says the following item is absent, so its letter is taken away

parts.note: T is time, the letter taken out of the previous word

explanation.surface: An empty purse with nothing in it, and no time to fill it.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash separates the definition from the fodder; 'time' is T, removed from EMPTY before the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A purse is the sum offered to winners of a boxing match or race, a prize fund.

clue.text: Yardstick that's abandoned right for English mathematician

indicators.note: one letter is abandoned and another put in its place, a straight swap

parts.note: a yardstick is a measuring rule
R is right, the letter dropped
E is English, the letter put in

explanation.surface: A standard rejected in favour of an English mathematician.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an English mathematician, but 'English' only supplies E; the answer is Swiss.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler was an eighteenth-century Swiss scholar famous for work in analysis and number theory.

clue.text: Reinvention of wheel's before finding particular alternative

indicators.note: reinventing something makes it anew in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive read as a plain plural
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: Reinventing the wheel is the proverbial waste of effort before finding a better option.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'wheel's' is ignored, so the fodder is WHEELS.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in some other place, so it points to an alternative location rather than here.

clue.text: Cold after a day over a huge area

indicators.note: coming after means following on, so this letter goes behind the earlier material

parts.note: A plus FRI, the abbreviation for Friday
C is cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A cold snap after a single day spreads across a big region.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'over' places what comes before above what follows, so the charade reads straight down.
explanation.definitionFit: The second-largest continent covers some thirty million square kilometres, certainly an enormous region.

clue.text: Not exactly small: swell shed!

parts.note: S is small, as in clothing sizes
a swell is a dandy or posh person, a toff

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a garden shed is not really small but big.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' is the old noun for a fashionable gentleman, a toff in British slang, and 'shed' is a verb, not an outbuilding.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed clothing or skin is to discard it, and the phrasal verb means throw aside.

clue.text: Eavesdroppers making a point?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: people listening in secretly to others
setter's reading: things dropping from the eaves of a roof and tapering to a sharp tip

explanation.walkthrough: Split 'eavesdroppers' into eaves and droppers: frozen drips hang from the roof edge and taper to a point.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen spikes of water hang from gutters and roof edges, each narrowing to a sharp tip.

clue.text: Second last?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to support, as in seconding a motion

definitions.note: adjective, as in the rear row
definitions.meaning: second meaning: at the rear, as in the rearmost seats

explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' and 'last' look like positions in a list, but the first is the verb meaning to support.
explanation.definitionFit: To support a proposal is to endorse it, and the rearmost row of seats is the final one.

clue.text: Divine in the distance summit that's not too demanding

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so these letters go within the other word

parts.note: DD is Doctor of Divinity, a divine or clergyman
the brow is the top of a hill

explanation.surface: A holy mountain top seen far off that is an easy climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' looks like an adjective or a verb but is the noun for a clergyman, abbreviated as the degree DD.
explanation.definitionFit: Middlebrow culture is accessible and undemanding, sitting between highbrow and lowbrow tastes.

clue.text: Thirty odd covers go with the Queen song

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap around it, so one piece encloses another
odd means strange or out of the ordinary, so the letters take an unusual order

parts.note: the word itself, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: About thirty cover versions of a royal song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thirty odd' looks like 'about thirty', but odd is the anagram signal, and 'covers' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: I Got Rhythm is a Gershwin standard from 1930, a well-known jazz tune.

clue.text: Slang somehow combined with fair mix of tongues

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged in an unstated order

explanation.surface: Slang blended with something fair produces a jumble of languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongues' means languages, here French and English.
explanation.definitionFit: Franglais is French heavily sprinkled with English words, a hybrid blending two languages.

clue.text: Very far from the rolling downs?

definitions.text: Very far from the rolling downs?

parts.words: Very far from the rolling downs?
parts.note: surface reading: somewhere a long way from hilly chalk countryside; setter's reading: rolling in it means very rich, so very far from that is utterly penniless, and the opposite of rolling land is level

explanation.walkthrough: The South Downs are rolling hills in England; land far from rolling is level, and someone far from rolling in money has none.
explanation.definitionFit: Being completely without money is the opposite of rolling in it, the idiom for being rich.

clue.text: Boy of mine employee refused tips

indicators.note: refusing the tips means turning away both ends, so the outer letters go

parts.note: a collier is a coal miner

explanation.surface: A young miner turned down gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' reads as gratuities but means the two ends of the word, C and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy's name, the short form of Oliver, fits the crossword convention of boy as any male name.

clue.text: Entering plea there, decisively beaten

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so the answer lies within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A defendant goes into court and makes a plea, then loses decisively.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters span pLEA THERE Decisively, ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for thrashed, either by a belt or heavily in a game, a thorough defeat.

clue.text: Grant much spoken of

indicators.note: something spoken is said out loud, so the sound matters, not the spelling

explanation.surface: A generous grant that people talk about a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' could be a noun or a name; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant something is to give or assign it, which is what apportioning a share means.

clue.text: Critical of small boy before gym class

indicators.note: before means ahead of, so the first part is placed in front of what follows

parts.note: rate means class, as in first-rate

explanation.surface: A teacher being scathing about a little lad ahead of PE.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Critical' looks like fault-finding, but it means dire, and 'small boy' is a shortened name.
explanation.definitionFit: A critical or desperate situation is extremely serious, near crisis point, so the adjectives match.

clue.text: Bind novel with cover raised higher

indicators.note: raised in a down answer means lifted upward, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: Emma is the Jane Austen novel

explanation.surface: Binding a book with its cover set higher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bind' looks like a bookbinding verb, but it is the noun, a tight spot; 'higher' places the cover above the novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a bind means facing an awkward predicament, a difficult choice between options.

clue.text: Bearing unhealthy resemblance to old Soviet symbol?

definitions.note: of a bearing or appearance, sickly means unhealthy
definitions.meaning: first meaning: having an ailing look

definitions.note: a jokey adjective, like a sickle
definitions.meaning: second meaning: sickle-like, after the hammer and sickle

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is whimsical: adding -ly to sickle gives an adjective for sickle-like, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone looking pale and weak appears sickly, and a curved blade shape is jokingly sickle-like.

clue.text: Help with crib at refurbished maternity unit, typically

indicators.note: refurbishing a place remakes it, so the letters are rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: Assistance with cots in a hospital ward for newborns that has been done up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Typically' marks the definition as an example: a maternity unit is one kind of place where people are born.
explanation.definitionFit: Hospital labour wards are where many babies arrive, so they are an example of where someone was born.

clue.text: When rook soars, catches birds that can't

indicators.note: a rook is R in chess, and soaring means rising, so in a down answer that letter climbs to the top

parts.note: to catch a remark is to hear it

explanation.surface: A rook takes off and catches birds that are unable to fly.
explanation.walkthrough: The R at the end of HEARS moves up to the top; 'birds that can't' means birds that can't soar.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheas are large flightless South American birds, related to ostriches and emus, so they cannot soar.

clue.text: Party organiser with cheering word

explanation.surface: The host of a celebration arrives with a cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' suggests a celebration, but it is a political party.
explanation.definitionFit: A whip is the official who keeps a parliamentary party's members in line and ensures they vote.

clue.text: One getting ready to go, indeed must stay in

indicators.note: to stay in is to remain inside, so one word sits within another

parts.note: to go is a euphemism for urinating

explanation.surface: Someone getting ready to leave is told they must stay indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is slang for cash (readies), and 'go' is the polite word for relieving oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready means cash, so the recipient of a payment is someone receiving money.

clue.text: Sign seen at hen party?

parts.note: surface reading: a banner or notice at a bride's pre-wedding celebration; setter's reading: a hen party has no male guests at all, so the letter for zero followed by the males who are absent

explanation.walkthrough: A hen party is a women-only celebration before a wedding; zero is O, so no men becomes O MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent or augury foretells what is coming, just as a sign of things to come does.

clue.text: Drive after leaving motorway initially required some guts!

indicators.note: once something has left it is no longer there, so that letter is removed
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: A driver needed courage once they came off the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guts' looks like courage, but it is literal: the omentum is part of the abdomen.
explanation.definitionFit: The omentum is a fold of peritoneum hanging from the stomach, a part of the abdominal viscera.

clue.text: A favourite of Henry I reputedly beat at game

definitions.text: A favourite of Henry I reputedly

explanation.surface: A royal favourite of an English king beat him at a sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Favourite' suggests a courtier, but Henry I is said to have died from eating a surfeit of these eel-like fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend holds the English king died after gorging on these jawless eel-like fish, so it was his favourite dish.

clue.text: A pushover? Yes, am hammered each time!

indicators.note: something hammered is battered out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: EA is the abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: Someone admits to being a soft touch because they get drunk every time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammered' reads as drunk, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone easily beaten or fooled is a soft target, the British idiom for an easy victim.

clue.text: Nervous, I thank God: peace finally!

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
DG is Deo gratias, Latin for thanks be to God

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept

explanation.surface: A jittery person sighs with relief when calm finally arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I thank God' looks like a whole exclamation, but I is ONE and 'thank God' is the Latin abbreviation DG.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tense and jumpy is the idiom's meaning, so it matches anxious or jittery exactly.
